title: What to Check Before You Use Modalyst for Private Label Products
excerpt: A private label readiness checklist: brandable surfaces, minimums, packaging control, sample verification, intellectual property checks, and margin that survives branded costs.
body: Private label is a promise about the product and not a logo added to a listing. If a buyer opens the box expecting a branded experience and receives a generic mailer with someone else's paperwork inside, the brand you were building takes the damage. Before committing to private label on a marketplace catalog, check the specific surfaces you can actually control and confirm each one with a physical sample.

Start with what can carry your brand. Neck labels, hang tags, packaging, inserts, and custom tape are the usual candidates, and each has different minimums, lead times, and cost behavior at low volume. Ask which are available per product rather than per supplier, because availability usually varies by item. A brandable label on a product with a twelve unit minimum is a very different commitment from the same label on something that requires two hundred.

Confirm the packaging and paperwork details that leak the supply chain. Some suppliers ship with invoices showing the wholesale price, others include their own marketing material, and a few will ship under a neutral or a branded return address on request. None of this appears in a product feed, and all of it is visible to the customer. Order one sample to your own address and a second to a different address to check whether the experience is consistent.

Verify quality at the sample stage and again after a real order. The first sample is the version a supplier wants you to see, which is exactly why the second one matters. Compare fabric, print placement, stitching, and sizing against the listing description, and be specific about tolerances. A size chart that is off by an inch is a returns problem you are about to buy at scale, and it is far cheaper to find in week one than in month three.

Do the intellectual property work before the design goes to print. Marketplace catalogs contain plenty of licensed and lookalike material, and private label puts your name on whatever you sell. Check trademarks for the brand name you plan to use, confirm the artwork is yours or properly licensed, and keep a record of those checks. It is unglamorous work, and it is also the part that decides whether you still have a business in a year.

Run the margin with private label costs included. Branding adds unit cost, minimums tie up cash, and samples become a real line item when you are testing several products. Add all of it to landed cost, then check whether the branded version supports a price your market will pay. Private label only works when the higher price holds, and the way to know is to test it on a small batch before scaling spend behind it.

Private label fits sellers who already know what they sell and to whom. It is a poor fit for the earliest testing phase, where speed and low commitment matter more than brand surface.
